html:
The Constitution of Bhutan, signed in Thimphu on 18 July 2008, made Bhutan a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, ending a century of rule by the Wangchuck kings as absolute monarchs.

The change came from the throne, not from the street. King Jigme Singye Wangchuck pushed it on a hesitant people, then gave up the crown in 2006 to his son, Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck. The first national elections were held in March 2008.

The constitution lets parliament, backed by a referendum, remove a king, and requires him to retire at 65. It also writes in some of the country's ideals: Gross National Happiness as a goal of the state, and forest to cover at least 60 per cent of the land. Critics note that the Nepali-speaking refugees expelled around 1990 had no part in it.
sum: The Constitution of Bhutan, signed in Thimphu on 18 July 2008, made Bhutan a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, ending a century of rule by the Wangchuck kings as absolute monarchs.
